content: Thomas Richard Allinson (1858–1918) was a British physician who strongly advocated for the consumption of whole grain bread, also known as wholemeal bread. His name remains associated with a popular bread brand in Europe, Allinson bread. Thomas Allinson was born in Grange-over-Sands, located in Morecambe Bay, Lancashire. At the age of fifteen, he began working as an assistant in a pharmacy. Using the money he saved from this job, along with financial support from his stepfather, he was able to enroll in medical school at the University of Edinburgh. By the age of 21, he had established his own medical practice in London. During the 1880s, Allinson developed a theory he called Naturopathy. This approach emphasized achieving health through proper diet and exercise rather than relying on conventional medicine. He particularly promoted the health benefits of stone-ground whole grain bread. Allinson authored and sold numerous books on topics such as stomach diseases, rheumatism, vegetarian cooking, and healthy diets. He also delivered public lectures to promote his ideas. In one of his books, The Advantages of Wholemeal Bread, he argued that whole grain bread was nutritionally superior to white, refined bread. He also advocated for vegetarianism and was one of the first to suggest that smoking was a cause of lung cancer, a groundbreaking idea at the time. Allinson actively sought public attention for his theories, often bypassing his medical colleagues to address the general public directly. This approach, along with his commercial ventures such as selling books, brought him into conflict with the English Royal College of Physicians and the General Medical Council. These institutions disapproved of his dissemination of controversial ideas to laypeople. By 1892, tensions had escalated. That year, under the motto Health Without Medicine, Allinson founded The Natural Food Company, which aimed to sell healthy foods. To support this endeavor, he purchased a grain mill in Bethnal Green to produce whole grain flour using traditional stone-grinding methods, as opposed to the roller milling process used for mass production. He later established a bakery as well. However, the Royal College of Physicians deemed running a food company incompatible with the role of a physician. As a result, Allinson was removed from the medical register and was no longer allowed to practice medicine. Despite this setback, his work gained recognition during World War I, when the nutritional value of whole grain bread was acknowledged. He was offered the opportunity to rejoin the medical registry, but he declined. Instead, his company thrived due to the increased demand for whole grain bread and flour. After his death, the company continued to grow, acquiring two additional stone-grinding mills in Newport, Monmouthshire, and Castleford, Yorkshire, in 1921. These mills remain operational to this day. Allinson's original bread recipe, which consisted of 100% whole grain flour, no added fat, less yeast, and more water, is still in use today. However, some enthusiasts of Allinson bread have noted that the bread is not as robust as it once was. Since the 1980s, the brand has used the advertising slogan Bread wi' nowt taken out.
